title: Get to know change
hook: study how all things change into one another (Meditations 10.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was arena, and Marcus's six names to keep. Your line was keep the name.

Take one photo of the same tree every week for a year, and the strip of pictures tells a story no single photo can. Buds, leaves, gold, bare branches, snow. It never stops changing; we just don't look closely enough to see it happen. In book ten Marcus treats watching change closely as a discipline of its own, a part of philosophy to train in.
screen: `ONE TREE, EVERY WEEK.` → `IT NEVER STOPS.` → `GET TO KNOW CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Learn the way of looking that sees how all things change into one another, Marcus writes. Keep attending to it, and train yourself in this part of philosophy. Nothing, he says, is so fitted to produce greatness of mind. Someone who really sees that everything is changing loosens their grip. They stop clutching, because there's nothing to clutch that will hold still. That person, he says, has in a way already set the body aside, knowing they must leave the human world, no one knows how soon. They give themselves wholly to justice in what they do, and to the nature of the whole in everything else. What others say or think or do against them doesn't occupy them. Two things are enough for them: to act justly now, and to be content with what is given now. And the week, looking back: correct or be kind, the smallest thing, let me not fear, simple and whole, made to bear it, keep the name, and now, study change. Under all seven lies the same ground: things are moving. People change, troubles end, prayers turn, names slip and come back. Watch change closely, and you hold everything a little more lightly, and act a little more justly. Marcus calls that greatness of mind, and he thinks you build it by looking.
screen: `SEE HOW ALL THINGS CHANGE.` · `IT BUILDS GREATNESS OF MIND.` · `JUSTICE NOW, CONTENT NOW.` · `A WEEK OF THINGS MOVING.` · then, large: `STUDY CHANGE.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at something that is changing right now: a cloud, a candle flame, a cup of tea cooling, light moving across a wall, your own breath. Just watch it change, second by second, and when your mind wanders, come back to the change. Notice how much is happening in what looked still.
Marcus, who trained himself to watch how all things change into one another, calling it a discipline that builds greatness of mind. Today's word.
Your line: study change. Nothing holds still, and seeing that loosens the grip. Another week, done.

howItsDone: Some Stoic readers practice contemplating change, watching a flame, a season or their own body, as a way to hold things more lightly and to stay focused on acting justly now.
